name: Wheel offset
seoTitle: Wheel offset Calculator: Free, With Steps
seoDesc: Wheel offset: work out inner distance old from the width and the offset. A free everyday life calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Wheel offset calculator turns the width, the offset and more into inner distance old. That makes it useful for a practical question that turns up in daily life. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Wheel offset calculator work?
sections.html:
The Wheel offset calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports inner distance old in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the width (Current wheel), the offset (Current wheel), the clearance change and the outer distance new.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Wheel offset calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Inner distance old=offset + (1 ÷ 2) × width
Offset=inner distance new − 1 ÷ 2 × width
Inner distance old=clearance change + inner distance new
Outer distance old=-offset + (1 ÷ 2) × width
Offset=-outer distance new + (1 ÷ 2) × width
Position change=-outer distance new + outer distance old

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Width = 30 in and Offset = 30 mm. Working through the relationship above gives Inner distance old = 45 in and Outer distance old = -15 in.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Inner distance old = 45 in and Outer distance old = -15 in should be roughly the size you expected from Width = 30 in and Offset = 30 mm.

Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Wheel offset calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the width, the offset and the clearance change — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Wheel offset calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns inner distance old, derived from the width, the offset and the clearance change. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Wheel offset calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the width, the offset, the clearance change and the outer distance new, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter width (Current wheel) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Width (Current wheel) opens in inches and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Inner distance old = 45 in. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Wheel offset calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
